title: Supermassive black holes may be wandering through galaxies after violent mergers
excerpt: New research on 100,000 quasars suggests supermassive black holes may be pushed away from galactic centers following powerful mergers.
content:
New research on 100,000 quasars suggests supermassive black holes may be pushed away from galactic centers following powerful mergers.

Supermassive black holes usually sit at the centers of large galaxies, where their enormous gravity influences the movement of nearby stars and gas. But some may not stay in those positions.

Powerful events following galactic mergers can send these massive objects moving away from their original locations.

Scientists have suspected this for years, but finding convincing evidence has been difficult.

Black holes do not produce light themselves, and other activity inside galaxies can make their movements hard to identify.

A new study involving approximately 100,000 quasars has found statistical evidence that some supermassive black holes may have been pushed away from galactic centers following mergers.

The findings also suggest that these events could be more common than previously established.

When black holes collide

Most large galaxies contain a central supermassive black hole with a mass millions or billions of times greater than the Sun.

When galaxies merge, their black holes can gradually move toward each other, form a pair and eventually combine into one larger black hole.

During this process, the black holes release gravitational waves, which are disturbances in space and time predicted by Albert Einstein’s theory of general relativity.

If the waves carry more energy in one direction than another, the newly formed black hole receives a powerful push in the opposite direction.

This recoil can send it traveling at several million miles per hour, potentially far from the galactic center.

A black hole that cannot settle down

Not every displaced black hole escapes its galaxy. Some remain trapped by the galaxy’s gravity and eventually return toward the center.

As they approach the center, they accelerate. They then pass through it, slow down farther away and reverse direction.

This movement can continue for a long time, although interactions with surrounding matter gradually reduce the motion.

Astronomers have previously identified individual black holes that might have experienced such events.

However, other physical processes can produce similar observations, making it difficult to confirm any particular case.

Finding clues in quasar light

Dr. Bence Bécsy is an assistant professor at the University of Birmingham and a graduate of Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE).

His team examined whether a much larger collection of observations could provide stronger evidence.

Their study analyzed approximately 100,000 quasars from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey.

Quasars are exceptionally bright galactic centers powered by supermassive black holes consuming surrounding gas.

The researchers measured differences in light emitted by gas near the black hole and gas farther away. These differences helped estimate the black hole’s movement relative to its galaxy.

They also examined how red each quasar appeared, since surrounding dust can absorb more blue light and make the remaining light appear redder.

Dust reveals a possible connection

The researchers found that quasars containing faster-moving black holes tended to appear redder. This suggests that those black holes were surrounded by greater amounts of dust.

The strongest difference appeared among the dustiest objects.

Heavily dust-obscured quasars were three times more common among those containing the fastest-moving black holes than among those with the slowest-moving black holes.

This relationship matches a prediction made in 2016 by Peter Raffai, Zoltán Haiman and Zsolt Frei.

The team’s computer models suggested that displaced black holes should move fastest near galactic centers, where dust concentrations are generally higher.

“We have now detected in real observational data the relationship we predicted years ago. It is difficult to think of a better example of why being a researcher is so rewarding,” said Raffai.

“Our findings may help us understand the processes taking place in galactic nuclei and the role played by Einstein’s gravitational waves in these processes.”

Why thousands of quasars matter

Individual quasars vary considerably in brightness, dust content and gas movement.

These differences can hide evidence of black hole recoil when astronomers examine objects separately.

By studying a large population, the researchers could identify a statistical relationship that would otherwise be difficult to detect.

“It is very difficult to prove that the black hole in a single quasar has been ejected, because other phenomena can produce similar signatures,” said Dr. Bécsy.

“What is new about our research is that, rather than looking for individual candidates, we searched statistically for traces of an entire population. This enabled us to identify a relationship consistent with theoretical predictions.”

Testing the evidence

The team repeated its analysis using different methods for selecting quasars and measuring their properties. The relationship remained consistent across these tests.

However, when researchers examined only gas clouds that do not follow the black hole’s movement, the positive relationship disappeared.

This result supports the possibility that the observed pattern is connected to moving black holes.

If the interpretation is correct, roughly half of the quasars studied may have experienced a relatively recent merger between two supermassive black holes.

The researchers caution that this estimate remains uncertain, and other explanations cannot yet be ruled out.

Preparing for the next gravitational-wave observatory

The findings could help astronomers estimate how frequently supermassive black holes merge and how their movements affect surrounding galaxies.

They could also inform preparations for the European Space Agency’s Laser Interferometer Space Antenna, or LISA, scheduled for launch in 2035.

The observatory will consist of three spacecraft separated by approximately 1.55 million miles, designed to detect gravitational waves from massive black hole mergers.

Bécsy also participates in the NANOGrav collaboration, which uses signals from pulsars to study extremely low-frequency gravitational waves. Evidence for these waves was first reported in 2023.

A long-running effort to understand black holes

ELTE researchers have contributed to LISA preparations since 2006.

Their work will continue through the Kármán Tódor Space Science Mission-Driven National Laboratory, established under a new framework beginning in 2026.

Professor Frei is head of the HUN-REN–ELTE Extragalactic Astrophysics Research Group.

“If the signal is indeed caused by ejected black holes, then two supermassive black holes merged relatively recently in a significant proportion of quasars, meaning that these events are common,” said Professor Frei.

“This directly determines how many such events LISA may be able to detect. We put this idea forward at ELTE ten years ago, and now we have tested it ourselves, led by Bence Bécsy, who graduated from our university.”

“Few research groups are fortunate enough to maintain this kind of continuity.”

For now, the evidence remains statistical rather than definitive.

Future observations could establish whether these unusual movements really result from black hole mergers and reveal how often massive black holes lose their central positions.

The full study was published in the journal Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society.
